name: Bianca Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Brook Farm, my dad's place, 160 acres on the edge of Wellham. We keep 80 outdoor sows and grow potatoes on contract for a crisp factory, plus some barley for the pigs. My mornings are pigs: feeding, checking the farrowing huts, fixing the electric fence they always find a way through. Afternoons in the season it's the potato harvester, and in winter it's the store and the paperwork, which I do in a ledger at the kitchen table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The bank, to be blunt. When Dad died I took out a loan to buy my brother Marco's half, so on top of the house there's a land loan, and the payments eat most of what the pigs make. Luis drives the school bus to keep us steady, and we've got maybe two weeks of money put by. I'm good at this, the crisp factory's field man says my potatoes are the cleanest he sees, but being good doesn't pay the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I don't need another thing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change farming, and pigs still need feeding in the rain. I'd say that at the market and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my problems are the same ones I had this morning. The crisp factory's contract price, the feed price and the bank payment decide everything. AI being hype doesn't help a farm that's already tight. Being good at farming doesn't pay the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same, ledger and all. I'd sell the old potato grader rather than repair it and borrow my neighbour's when I need one. And I'd ask the bank for a payment holiday in the slow months if the pig price drops again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Tired and a bit scared, but used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the pig price drops, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sow numbers. I'd cull the ten oldest sows early and not replace them, which means less money next year, but less feed now. It's like eating your seed potatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to when it's tight like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Marco, funnily enough, even though he's the reason for the loan. He's an electrician in town and he'll come out on a Sunday to fix the pump for nothing. Family is the only safety net I trust.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, nicely, because pigs still need feeding in the rain.
I'd say every few years a **new thing** promises to change farming.
think: I think my problems stay the same: the **contract price**, feed and the bank.
AI being hype doesn't help a farm that's **already tight**.
do: Sell the **old potato grader** and borrow the neighbour's instead.
Ask the bank for a **payment holiday** in slow months if prices drop.
Keep the books in the **kitchen ledger** as always.
feel: **Tired** and a bit **scared**, but used to it.
S0.quote: Being good at farming doesn't pay the bank.
fieldNote: Bianca's pressure is **debt** from buying out her brother, before AI comes into it.
She's **resistant** and relieved there's nothing new to learn.
She trusts **family** above any institution, even the brother tied to the loan.
Her coping move is **cutting the herd**, which she knows costs next year's income.

steps.text: Sell the old potato grader and borrow the neighbour's
Keep the farm books in the kitchen ledger
Lean on Marco for Sunday repairs instead of paying a contractor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking jobs first. So the crisp factory's office changes and I keep doing my thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices and not much use for a pig farm. If someone at market asked, I'd say I'll look at it when it's proven, and not before. I wouldn't post anything, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the crisp factory would use it to squeeze us harder. Their buyer would have a program that knows every farm's costs and pays the least anyone will take. I'd lose the bit of bargaining I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming the same and refuse to put my records online, no matter what the factory says. I'd ask Luis to look at an extra school route. And I'd ask the neighbour, Alan, whether he wants to share the pig feed order to get a better price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the ground's shifting and nobody's told me where to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the crisp factory insists on records online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Sofia would do it for me, she's fourteen and does everything on her phone. I'd hate that. Brook Farm is my farm, and I'd be asking my daughter how to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until it's proven. What would prove it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work on a farm like mine, not a farm on the telly. If Alan used something for three years and it saved him money, I'd listen. Alan is more careful than me, which is saying something.

say: I'd say it's fine for offices and **not much use** for a pig farm.
I'd tell people at market I'll look at it **once it's proven**.
think: I think the **crisp factory** would use it to squeeze growers harder.
I'd lose the **bit of bargaining** I've got on price.
do: Refuse to put farm **records online**, whatever the factory says.
Ask Luis about an **extra school route** for more pay.
Share the **pig feed order** with neighbour Alan for a better price.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the ground is shifting and nobody's said **where to stand**.
S1.quote: Brook Farm is my farm, and I'd be asking my daughter how to run it.
fieldNote: Bianca sees the threat through the **buyer**: AI makes the crisp factory a tougher bargainer.
Her **pride** shows in hating to ask her daughter for help with records.
She'd only change if a **careful neighbour** proved it over years.
Income could shrink through **lower contract prices**, which keeps her anxious.

steps.text: Keep paper records and refuse to put them online
Share the pig feed order with Alan to cut the price
Wait for Alan to try any new tool for three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Robots by 2031. I'd be forty-eight. Sofia would be leaving school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort it out, fast, because farms like mine can't. At market I'd say it calmly, because that's how I am. But I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the potato contract within a year or two. The factory would deal with big growers who use AI for everything, and by 2031 the big growers have robot harvesters too. Then it's pigs only, and pigs alone can't pay the land loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd probably sell the twenty acres by the road, the ones the builder keeps asking about, to pay down the loan. Luis would take any extra driving he can get. I'm not going to learn computers at forty-five, I'd be no good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like when the vet says the word swine fever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Mateo that Brook Farm might not be his one day, and I don't know how to say that kindly. Sofia would want to help, she always does. Mateo would go quiet, that's his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the road acres. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. Selling the twenty acres Dad bought the year I was born would feel like selling a bit of him. But a loan doesn't care about feelings.

say: I'd say the **government** needs to sort it out fast, because small farms can't.
I'd say it **calmly** at market, but mean it.
think: I think I'd lose the **potato contract** within a year or two.
**Pigs alone** can't pay the land loan.
do: Sell the **twenty roadside acres** to the builder to cut the loan.
Ask Luis to take **any extra driving** he can get.
Refuse to **learn computers**, believing she'd be no good at it.
feel: **Sick**, like hearing the vet say **swine fever**.
S2.quote: Selling the twenty acres Dad bought the year I was born would feel like selling a bit of him.
fieldNote: Bianca expects to **lose the potato contract**, a big part of farm income.
Her only plan is to **sell land** her father bought, and it hurts her.
She refuses **retraining** out of low confidence, not just habit.
Telling her son the farm may not be his is the **hardest moment**.

steps.text: Sell the twenty roadside acres to the builder
Ask Luis to take every extra bus route going
Pay the land loan down with the sale money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Long enough to see it coming. Not long enough to do much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to know the rules early, like what happens to small contracts and loans. I'd say it to the farmers' union rep, who's a sensible man. I'd want somebody in charge to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same as the fast one, just slower. The factory moves to big growers around 2031, robots come in 2034, and I'm still holding a loan. The difference is that I'd see it coming, which might be worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a couple of years to see if it's real before doing anything big. Then I'd start cutting back on the potatoes and putting more into the pigs, which are harder for robots to handle out in the mud. And I'd ask the bank to stretch the land loan over more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, the slow grinding kind. Like waiting for test results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pigs over potatoes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Potatoes are already planted, sprayed and lifted by machines, but outdoor pigs are mud, weather and stubborn animals. From those machines it's a short step to robots. I'd bet on the mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said seeing it coming might be worse. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd lie awake doing sums for five years instead of two. I'm the sort who worries in advance. Luis says I pay for every problem twice.

say: I'd say we need **clear rules early** on small contracts and loans.
I'd want someone **in charge** to have a plan.
think: I think it's the fast picture **slowed down**, with the loan still there.
Seeing it coming might be **worse** for someone who worries ahead.
do: Wait **two years** to see if it's real before big changes.
Shift from **potatoes to pigs**, which robots handle worse in mud.
Ask the bank to **stretch the land loan** over more years.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow, grinding way, like **waiting for results**.
S3.quote: Potatoes are already planted, sprayed and lifted by machines, but outdoor pigs are mud, weather and stubborn animals.
fieldNote: Bianca still expects to **lose major income** around 2031, so alarm stays.
She makes one clever bet: **pigs over potatoes**, because mud is hard for robots.
Her **wait-and-see** habit returns when there's time.
She worries in advance; her husband says she **pays twice** for every problem.

steps.text: Wait two years to see if the change is real
Move acres from potatoes into more outdoor sows
Ask the bank to stretch the land loan over more years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. Mateo would be twenty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a plan, so let's have one. I'd ask the union rep what the plan is every time I saw him. I'm not a campaigner, but I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I might have the land loan mostly paid. If prices hold, I'd owe a lot less by 2036, and the kids would be grown. I'd still be worried, but it feels like there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for now. Maybe in five years I'd go and look at what Alan's doing, if he's using any of it. I'd put any good year's money into the loan, not the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Not easy, but easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good year look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Potatoes at a decent contract price, no disease in the sows, a dry harvest. Then I'd put five thousand into the loan. That's happened twice in eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Sofia set them up and I could see the point. I'm not against it, I just don't want to look a fool. I'd rather keep being the best potato grower round here than become a bad computer user.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough for a plan**, so we should have one.
I'd keep asking the **union rep** what the plan is.
think: I think ten years means the **land loan** might be mostly paid.
With the kids grown by then, there's **some time**.
do: Carry on **as she is** for the next few years.
Visit Alan in **five years** to see what tools he's using.
Put any **good year's money** into the loan, not the house.
S4.quote: I'd rather keep being the best potato grower round here than become a bad computer user.
fieldNote: The decade lets Bianca picture the **loan mostly paid** and the kids grown.
Her mood stays **anxious**: two good years in eight is thin ground.
Her resistance is partly **fear of looking foolish**, which she admits.

steps.text: Carry on farming the 80 sows and potatoes as now
Put any good year's surplus into the land loan
Visit Alan in five years to see his tools working

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose the potato contract and still have the loan, with no time to get the debt down. What would help is the bank giving farmers like me longer to pay, and somebody making sure the crisp factory keeps small growers on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. He worked this farm forty years. A farm is a family's whole history, and I'd hate to be the one who lost it.

headlineQuote: A farm is a family's whole history, and I'd hate to be the one who lost it.
portrait: Bianca runs her late father's pig and potato farm, carrying a **land loan**.
She took the loan to **buy out** her brother, and has two weeks of savings.
She's **pragmatic**, trusts family over institutions, and never uses AI tools.
She expects to lose the **potato contract** in the fast scenarios and would sell land.
Her mood runs **anxious to alarmed**, easing only with a decade to pay debt.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd lose the **potato contract** while still holding the loan.
whatWouldHelp: Longer **bank terms** for farmers and contracts kept open for **small growers**.
